_meta.description: Sigma canonical field -> per-platform field name. The rules are written against the canonical column, which is the vocabulary in telemetry/data-sources.md; nothing here changes a rule. Each platform's deployment maps it.
_meta.why: Sigma `EventID` vs Splunk `EventCode` vs Elastic `event.code` vs Kusto `EventID`. A missing alias makes a rule evaluate against a null field, which matches nothing, silently. That failure has no symptom - a rule that never fires looks like a quiet rule.
_meta.not_validated_against: A live Splunk, Elastic or Sentinel instance. These are the documented names for each platform, not names read back from a deployed index template.

EventID.note: Splunk parses Windows event logs as EventCode. This alias is the one that most often goes missing.

Computer.note: Splunk's Computer is usually populated; on forwarders without it, coalesce with host.

Image.note: Sysmon 1 Image. In Kusto's DeviceProcessEvents this is FolderPath; the full command is ProcessCommandLine.

ParentProcessGuid.note: The stage0->stage1 join key. Elastic's entity_id is not the same identifier as Sysmon's ProcessGuid - it must be derived at ingest, or the join in analytics/stage_join.py is expressed against whatever per-boot id the platform has.

ProcessGuid.note: Same caveat as ParentProcessGuid: a per-boot process identity, not the raw PID.

ObjectName.note: Security 4663 objects. Elastic routes registry objects to registry.path and file objects to file.path; a single 4663 rule needs a shared field or two queries.

AccessMask.note: Elastic's ECS has no field for a Windows access mask; the raw event data is the only place it exists.

TargetImage.note: Only meaningful on Sysmon 8/10. There is no ECS field for 'the process whose memory was touched' until process.target.* was added; verify against the deployment's ECS version.

Signature.note: Elastic resolves the signer to the certificate subject; Sysmon's Signature is the same value in most deployments but a self-signed or unverifiable binary is empty in both.

IntegrityLevel.note: Elastic's is a non-ECS extension field; it is present in the default Windows integration.

query.note: Zeek naming for the same object as QueryName. Two rules use one name and two the other; the map is what makes them the same on a platform.

Source.note: Zeek's Source. Splunk's `src` is only populated if the deployment maps it; the props.conf snippet in docs/deployment.md does.

SourceAddress.note: Proxy client address. Same canonical object as Zeek's Source, different exporter.

destination_port.note: Netflow naming for the same object as DestinationPort.

cs-user-agent.note: Splunk renames proxy fields: the hyphen becomes an underscore.

cs-uri-query.note: Kusto's RequestURL holds path and query together; a query-only rule needs split().

cs-header-X-Id.note: Requires full custom-header retention on the proxy. Elastic's field is only populated when the proxy emits headers as structured data, which most do not by default.

certificate.subject.note: Zeek x509 naming. Elastic's is the parsed common name, not the full DN string - a rule comparing full DNs needs the raw event data.

CertificateSelfSigned.note: Derived, not raw: self-signed means subject == issuer. Splunk and Kusto carry a boolean an EDR callback supplies; on Elastic the rule must compare subject to issuer, which is why this entry points at the issuer field.

CertificateSelfSigned.elastic: runtime field `CertificateSelfSigned`: emit(true) if tls.server.x509.subject.common_name == tls.server.x509.issuer.common_name
CertificateSelfSigned.why: Self-signed means subject equals issuer. Aliasing it to either one produces a string where a rule tests a boolean, so every comparison is silently false.
